content: 1. The study by Berkley-Patton et al. (2019) evaluated the feasibility and outcomes of an HIV testing intervention implemented in African American churches, as published in AIDS Behavior. 2. Blas et al. (2010) investigated the impact of an online video-based intervention on increasing HIV testing among men who have sex with men in Peru, as reported in PLoS ONE. 3. Brown et al. (2018) conducted a randomized controlled trial using behavioral insights to improve the return rates of HIV self-sampling kits in England, as detailed in HIV Medicine. 4. Cohan et al. (2009) compared patient perspectives on abbreviated versus standard pre-test HIV counseling in prenatal settings through a non-inferiority randomized controlled trial, published in PLoS ONE. 5. De Tolly et al. (2011) explored the use of short message services (SMS) to increase HIV testing uptake and assessed the impact of message content and dosage, as described in Telemedicine and e-Health. 6. Simpson et al. (1999) conducted a randomized controlled trial to evaluate different approaches to universal antenatal HIV testing, focusing on uptake and acceptability, as published in Health Technology Assessment. 7. Spielberg et al. (2013) examined the use of microfinance to influence HIV-related and financial behaviors among adolescents and their mothers in West Bengal through a cluster randomized trial, as reported in International Journal of Adolescent Medicine and Health. 8. Van Heerden et al. (2015) conducted a mixed-methods study to locate men within a home-based counseling and testing program in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa, highlighting the challenges of male participation, as published in the African Journal of AIDS Research. 9. Wang et al. (2018) evaluated the efficacy of promoting home-based HIV self-testing with online counseling to increase testing rates among men who have sex with men, as detailed in AIDS Behavior. 10. Kelvin et al. (2019) assessed the impact of announcing the availability of oral HIV self-test kits via text messages to increase testing among hard-to-reach truckers in Kenya, as reported in BMC Public Health. 11. Salyers-Bull et al. (2004) described the recruitment and retention strategies for an online sample in an HIV prevention intervention targeting men who have sex with men, as part of the Smart Sex Quest project, published in AIDS Care. 12. Choko (2016) conducted a trial investigating multiple interventions to increase HIV testing and linkage to care for male partners of pregnant women attending antenatal clinics through self-testing, as documented by the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine. 13. Choko et al. (2019) evaluated HIV self-testing with or without additional interventions, including financial incentives, to improve linkage to care among male partners of antenatal care attendees in Malawi, as published in PLoS Medicine. 14. Wanyenze et al. (2013) conducted a factorial randomized controlled trial in Uganda to assess abbreviated HIV counseling and testing with enhanced referral to care, as reported in The Lancet Global Health. 15. Booth et al. (2011) examined strategies to reduce HIV-related risk behaviors among injection drug users in residential detoxification settings, as detailed in AIDS Behavior. 16. Metsch et al. (2012) implemented rapid HIV testing with or without risk-reduction counseling in drug treatment centers, reporting the results of a randomized trial in American Journal of Public Health. 17. McKee et al. (2011) piloted an intervention to improve sexually transmitted infection testing among urban adolescents, as published in Journal of Adolescent Health. 18. Dolcini et al. (2017) developed Project ÒRÉ, a friendship-based intervention aimed at preventing HIV/STI among urban African American adolescent females, as described in Health Education & Behavior. 19. Jiraphongsa et al. (2002) studied the acceptance of HIV testing and counseling among unmarried young adults in northern Thailand, as reported in AIDS Education and Prevention. 20. Ybarra et al. (2017) conducted a pilot randomized controlled trial to evaluate an mHealth HIV prevention program for sexual minority male adolescents, as published in Pediatrics. 21. Firestone et al. (2016) evaluated the impact of intensive group learning and on-site services on improving sexual and reproductive health among young adults in Liberia, as detailed in Global Health Science and Practice. 22. Festinger et al. (2016) examined the efficacy of a computer-facilitated HIV prevention tool in drug court settings, as reported in Drug and Alcohol Dependence. 23. Uhrig et al. (2012) assessed the efficacy of an HIV testing campaign targeting African American women, focusing on the campaign's messaging, as published in Health Marketing Quarterly. 24. Derksen et al. (2015) conducted a cluster-randomized trial in Malawi to reduce stigma and increase HIV testing through a health information intervention, as reported in Journal of the International AIDS Society. 25. Apanovitch et al. (2003) explored the use of message framing to motivate HIV testing among low-income, ethnic minority women, as detailed in Health Psychology. 26. Mikolajczak et al. (2012) evaluated an online HIV prevention intervention aimed at promoting HIV testing among men who have sex with men through a randomized controlled trial, as published in Netherlands Journal of Psychology. 27. Simbayi et al. (2004) implemented theory-based HIV risk reduction counseling for sexually transmitted infection clinic patients in Cape Town, South Africa, as reported in Sexually Transmitted Diseases. 28. Carey et al. (2008) conducted a randomized controlled trial to improve HIV rapid testing rates among STD clinic patients, as detailed in Health Psychology. 29. Bentz et al. (2010) evaluated the outcomes of counseling on adherence to prophylaxis and follow-up after sexual HIV-risk exposure through a randomized controlled trial, as published in AIDS Care. 30. Edelman et al. (2013) studied HIV testing and sexual risk reduction counseling in office-based buprenorphine/naloxone treatment settings, as reported in Journal of Addiction Medicine. 31. Diallo et al. (2010) assessed the efficacy of a single-session HIV prevention intervention for Black women through a group randomized controlled trial, as detailed in AIDS Behavior. 32. Merchant et al. (2015) identified factors influencing the uptake of rapid HIV and hepatitis C screening among drug-misusing adult emergency department patients, with implications for future interventions, as published in AIDS Behavior. 33. Kalichman et al. (1993) evaluated culturally tailored HIV-AIDS risk-reduction messages targeting African-American urban women, focusing on risk sensitization and reduction, as reported in Journal of Consulting and Clinical Psychology. 34. Kalichman and Coley (1995) explored the use of context framing to enhance HIV-antibody-testing messages for African American women, as detailed in Health Psychology. 35. Cordova (2018) assessed the preliminary efficacy of an HIV preventive intervention app in an urban youth-centered community health clinic, as published in Journal of Adolescent Health. 36. Exner et al. (2002) examined women's experiences with HIV counseling and testing and the perceived role of testing as a prevention strategy, as reported in Perspectives on Sexual and Reproductive Health.
